title: From “brain drain” to “brain gain”: The case for global skill partnerships in healthcare

From “brain drain” to “brain gain”: The case for global skill partnerships in healthcare

Limon Bade Rodriguez

Pablo Acosta

November 06, 2026

This page in:

When designed well, Global Skill Partnerships can transform a global health worker shortage into a development opportunity. | © Shutterstock.com

The world faces a shortfall of approximately 15 million health workers. Yet in lower-income countries, many people who could fill these jobs lack the training that would make them competitive at home or abroad. Global Skill Partnerships (GSPs) were designed to close this gap. They finance training in the worker's home country, then place graduates either in domestic jobs (the "home" track) or in safe, orderly, and legal jobs abroad (the "abroad" track). When they work, everyone gains. Sending and receiving countries strengthen their health workforces, workers build skills while their families benefit from higher incomes.
Building on an earlier blog introducing GSPs, this post draws on a review of existing programs, labor mobility schemes in Asia and the Pacific, and frameworks including the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Code of Practice and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations' (ASEAN) mutual recognition agreements. It assesses what the evidence says about GSPs' effectiveness in delivering quality jobs at home and abroad, and what policymakers should consider before adopting the model in the health sector.
 
Key insights from the analysis:
1. From “brain drain” to “brain gain.” Emigration of skilled workers is a valid concern, especially in Africa and small island developing states. However, evidence points to potential “brain gain” through at least three mechanisms. GSPs reduce “brain drain” by design. Under the Philippines-Germany GSP, as of April 2025, more than 300 nurses had been trained or were in training, with almost 200 working or planning to work in the Philippines through the “home” track. Prospects for working abroad raise expected returns to health professional education, spurring investment in training in origin countries, particularly by the private sector. In the Philippines, migration incentives were associated with nine additional nurses licensed domestically for every nurse who migrated to the United States. Diasporas further support worker pipelines at home; the German-Kosovar diaspora invested in Heimerer Medical College in Kosovo, with majority of the graduates working domestically.

2. Skill recognition reduces “brain waste.” Early in Germany’s labor mobility program in healthcare, known as the Triple Win, nurses from sending countries waited up to two years for full accreditation, working below their qualifications at lower salaries. The GSP model sought to address this issue by requiring language training and credentials to be completed before departure, so participants arrive already recognized as fully qualified nurses, with access to higher salaries—compared to nurses whose qualifications are not fully recognized in destination countries—, professional development, and pathways to family reunification and residency. Canada’s recognition of nursing qualifications from Aga Khan University in Pakistan offers another model GSPs could adapt.
 
3. Co-investment delivers proportional benefits. The 2026 amendments to the WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel encourage co-investments in health systems for mutual benefit, aside from expanding the Code’s scope to include care workers. In the Philippines-Germany GSP, German employers finance not only the training, migration, and accreditation costs, but also modern equipment, curriculum upgrades, and scholarships in partner nursing schools. This also illustrates how employer financing and private capital can help expand the skill systems needed for jobs at home and abroad. The World Bank’s aged care GSPs - linking Colombia, Ecuador, and Dominican Republic with Spain, and Kenya with Canada - similarly co-invest in healthcare education and training systems in origin countries. The key principle: GSPs must respond to origin countries’ health and employment priorities to build political support.
 
4. Language training and integration are essential. The Philippines-Germany GSP provides advanced language training, and the fact that nurses on the "abroad" track stay with the same employer despite no employment bond suggests these investments support retention. Japan's programs facilitating nursing and caregiving from Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam, including Japanese language training—supported by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) through online portals, mobile apps, and migrant worker consultation services—point in the right direction.
 
5. South-South and intra-regional GSPs are growing. The scale of the global health worker shortage makes South-South and intra-regional GSPs just as important as traditional South-North programs. In the Pacific, labor mobility in aged care from Solomon Islands to Niue and in nursing from Papua New Guinea to Fiji are potential starting points; South Asia presents similar opportunities as Sri Lanka's working-age population peaks. Strengthening Papua New Guinea’s capacity to train nurses, for instance, could help meet demand both domestically and in neighboring Pacific countries. These programs can build on existing frameworks like ASEAN's mutual recognition agreements and Aga Khan University's nursing campuses in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. The World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and bilateral donors including the Belgian Development Agency are paying increasing attention to this model.
 
Policy recommendations
To deliver on their promise, GSPs in the healthcare sector need to:

Foster human capital accumulation in both origin and destination countries by creating enabling conditions for public and private investment in education and training

Ensure mutual benefit by linking GSPs to origin and destination countries’ health, education, and employment priorities, building political support through clear and tangible public benefits

Reduce “brain waste” by embedding skill recognition before international labor mobility begins, not after a multi-year waiting period upon arrival

Invest in integration through language training, housing support, and community engagement from the outset and in reintegration of returnees through employment assistance and social protection.  

When designed well, GSPs can transform a global health worker shortage into a development opportunity. For origin countries, they mean higher-quality training, greater availability of qualified health workers, stronger health systems, increased remittances, and diaspora investment. For destination countries, they mean a reliable, qualified, and integrated workforce.
